overview.body:
**Forseti** (*forseti*) — Justice, Mediation · Son of Baldr, Lord of Glitnir — is the settler of strife: the god who owns the hall of gold pillars and silver roof, and from whose seat, Snorri says, all who come with lawsuits go away reconciled — the best court of judgment among gods and men.[^1]

His dossier is the thinnest of any hall-owning Æsir: a single stanza of Grímnismál and a single sentence of Gylfaginning carry his whole mythology, and the þulur keep his name in the roll of the gods.[^2] He is the son of [[baldr|Baldr]] and [[nanna|Nanna]], daughter of Nep — the child of the god whose own judgments, Snorri notes, could never stand.[^1] Four centuries before the Eddic manuscripts, Alcuin's Life of Willibrord records the Frisian cult of Fosite on the island Fosetesland (Heligoland), with its silent spring and sacred cattle — the continental witness whose equation with Forseti remains the standing question of the scholarship.[^3]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Forseti** — identical to the ASCII input, because the normalized Old Norse form is itself plain ASCII: no diacritic, no distinctive letter, nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The name is therefore Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule — a property of its orthography, not of the god's standing. The plain-ASCII domain forseti.com is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release; the project claims no domain for this temple.[^4]

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Old Norse as **Forseti** (nominative; genitive *Forseta* — a weak masculine in -i, which is why the name takes no nominative -r). It is a transparent Old Norse compound: *for* ‘before’ + *seti* ‘sitter’ (cf. *sitja*, ‘to sit’) — ‘the one who sits before’, hence the common noun *forseti*, ‘chairman, president’, used as a law-term of the judge who presides over a court.[^1] The god's name is the office made personal: the presiding one.

The etymological transparency is itself the crux of the Fosite question. Frisian *Fosite*, attested by Alcuin around 796 — four centuries before the Eddic manuscripts — cannot be derived from Old Norse *forseti*; scholars since Grimm have therefore entertained that the Norse god was borrowed from the Frisian cult and re-etymologized into a law-term on the way north, and Lindow keeps the question open rather than settled.[^2]

The ASCII form is not a compromise here: normalized Old Norse *Forseti* is already written in plain ASCII letters. There is no diacritic, no thorn or eth, no vowel-length mark for the early domain-name system to have stripped. The name is classified Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule — the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses — which is a statement about orthography, never about the god.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **f** → **F** — Same, capitalized
- **o** → **o** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **s** → **s** — Same
- **e** → **e** — Same
- **t** → **t** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same

The project holds no domain for this name: **forseti.com** is registered to a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release. The temple lives at its canonical lexicon address.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈfor.se.ti/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **For-** — Voiceless labiodental [f], short open-mid back [ɔ], trilled [r]; the preposition *for*, ‘before’, stressed on the first syllable as in every Old Norse word
- **-se-** — Voiceless alveolar fricative [s] and short front [ɛ]; all three vowels of the name are short, and the orthography marks no length anywhere
- **-ti** — Voiceless dental stop [t] and short close front [i]; the final *-i* is the weak masculine ending, so the name carries no nominative *-r*

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ‘FOR-seh-ti’ — three short, even syllables, stress on the first, the r lightly trilled; close to the modern Icelandic pronunciation of *forseti*, ‘president’.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Forseti, the theonym and the law-term, ‘chairman, president’
- **Old Frisian** — Fosite, the god of Fosetesland (Heligoland) in Alcuin's Life of Willibrord, c. 796[^2]
- **Younger Futhark** — ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ, the reconstructed Viking-Age runic rendering
- **Modern Icelandic** — Forseti, the god's name and the title of the President of Iceland

Forseti is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing ASCII cannot carry: no accent, no distinctive letter, no length mark. The dignity of the name is in the office it names, not in rescued diacritics.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi 10, ed. Levison, MGH SRM 7 (1920).

domains.body:
**Forseti** governs Justice and Mediation — and the sources earn both terms in a single sentence each.[^1]

### Justice

Snorri calls his seat the best court of judgment — *dómstaðr* — among gods and men: the one bench in the cosmos whose rulings no one leaves disputing.

### Mediation

Grímnismál's verb is *svæfir* — he ‘puts to sleep’, lulls, every suit: reconciliation, not verdict, is the office. All who come with their cases go away *sáttir*, reconciled.

### The Hall of Glitnir

‘The shining one’ — propped with gold, roofed with silver — is the Edda's architecture of justice: the court as the brightest building in heaven.

### The Title

*Forseti*, ‘he who sits before’: the god is the office of the presiding judge made personal — the one law-term in the pantheon that walks and reigns.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 32; Grímnismál 15, trans. Faulkes (1987) and Larrington (2014).

symbols.body:
The iconography of Forseti is architectural and procedural — the corpus gives him no regalia, no weapon, and no animal, but fixed around his hall a small set of attributes:[^1]

- **Glitnir** — ‘The shining one’, the hall propped with gold and roofed with silver: justice as the brightest building in heaven
- **The dómstaðr** — The judgment-seat Snorri calls the best among gods and men: authority measured in reconciled parties, not in sentences
- **Sátt, the settlement** — The reconciled departure: the Edda's one statistic about the god, that all who come with suits go away at peace
- **The silent spring** — The holy water of Fosetesland, drawn only in silence: the Frisian face of the settler of strife, if the equation holds[^2]
- **The title forseti** — ‘He who sits before’: the office that became a god, and the word that outlived him into a republic

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 17 and 32; Grímnismál 15, trans. Faulkes (1987) and Larrington (2014).
Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi 10, ed. Levison, MGH SRM 7 (1920).

mythology.body:
Forseti's mythology is the shortest in the Edda and the most complete: one stanza, one sentence, and the office they describe needs no plot. When the Prose Edda catalogues the sons of the gods, it gives him two facts and lets them stand: he is the son of [[baldr|Baldr]] and [[nanna|Nanna]], and his hall is the court from which no quarrel leaves alive.[^1]

### The Tenth Hall (Grímnismál 15)

Grímnismál counts the dwellings of the gods, and the tenth is his: ‘Glitnir is the tenth; it is propped with gold and thatched with silver too, and there Forseti dwells most days and puts all suits to sleep’ — *svæfir allar sakir*. The verb is the miracle: not wins, not crushes, but lulls to sleep, the way one settles a restless child.[^2]

### The Best Court Among Gods and Men (Gylfaginning 17 · 32)

Snorri builds the same hall twice — first among the heavenly places, with walls, pillars, and posts of red gold and a roof of silver; then among the Æsir, where he names the owner: the son of Baldr and Nanna, daughter of Nep, is called Forseti, and all who come to him with lawsuits go away reconciled. ‘That is the best court of judgment among gods and men, as it is said here’ — and Snorri quotes the Grímnismál stanza as his proof.[^1]

### The Inheritance

The corpus never stages the contrast, but it cannot be accidental: of Baldr, Snorri says that none of his judgments can stand; of Baldr's son, that no judgment of his is ever refused. The father's flaw is retired in the son's office — the god of light whom no settlement could save leaves behind the god who saves every settlement.[^1]

### The Name in the Roll

Beyond the stanza and the sentence, Forseti lives in the catalogues: the þulur count him among the Æsir, and no saga, skaldic stanza, or kenning-list ever stages him in action. The tradition treats him the way law treats a good judge: no stories, only the record that the court was held.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 17 and 32, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Grímnismál 15 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur of the Æsir, trans. Faulkes (1987).

syncretism.body:
The standing cross-border question is the equation Forseti = Fosite. Jacob Grimm made it, and the philology keeps it alive: Old Norse *forseti* is a transparent folk-formation — ‘the one who sits before’ — while the Frisian *Fosite* attested by Alcuin around 796 cannot be derived from it. Lindow therefore entertains that the Norse god was borrowed from the Frisian cult and re-etymologized into a law-term on the way north; the Norwegian place-name Forsetlund, ‘Forseti's grove’, shows the name lived in Scandinavian cult-geography whatever its direction of travel.[^1]

Within the corpus his true kin is [[tyr|Týr]], the pantheon's other god of law: where Týr guarantees the oath with his right hand in the wolf's jaws, Forseti dissolves the quarrel the oath was sworn to settle — pledge and mediation, the two mechanisms of northern law divided between two gods.[^2] Across traditions, the judge-gods keep their distance from him in character: Greek [[themis|Themis]] is law as cosmic ordinance and Egyptian [[maat|Ma'at]] is truth weighed against a feather, but Forseti is law as outcome — the verdict both parties can live inside. His closest figure in the household is his own father [[baldr|Baldr]], whose judgments could not stand, and [[hermod|Hermóðr]], whose errand for that father failed by a single refusal: the family of the shining god is the Edda's seminar on what justice cannot do, and Forseti is its one success.

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Forseti; Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Hall (D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Forseti, Fosite.
Grimm, Jacob, Teutonic Mythology, trans. James Steven Stallybrass, 4 vols. (London: George Bell, 1882–88), on Fosite and Forseti.

cultural-legacy.body:
Forseti's afterlife is the word itself. Old Norse *forseti* was the law-term for the presiding judge — the one who sits before the court — and when Iceland became a republic in 1944 it reached for the same word for its head of state: the President of Iceland is to this day *Forseti Íslands*, and no other god of the North still signs laws.[^1]

In scholarship, the god's single sentence in Gylfaginning became one of the most-quoted passages on the Norse legal imagination — the standing citation for the proposition that the North idealized reconciliation over verdict, the settlement over the sentence.[^2] Modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities keep him as the patron of mediation and of disputes ended without feud; and on the Frisian side, Heligoland — the holy land — still carries the memory of the cult in its name. He left no image, no saga, no drama: he left his title to a republic.

sources.citation: Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. forseti; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (1910), s.v. forseti.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Forseti.

archaeology.body:
Forseti is a textual and onomastic god: no runestone invokes him, no image or amulet names him, and no votive deposit can be laid at his hall.[^1] The ground evidence is the place-name: Forsetlund, ‘Forseti's grove’, in Vestfold near the Oslo fjord, attests that the name lived in Scandinavian cult-geography and not only in Icelandic books.[^2]

The Frisian witness is earlier than any Norse manuscript: Alcuin's Life of Willibrord, written around 796, preserves the island Fosetesland — Heligoland, ‘holy land’ — with its silent spring and sacred herd, the only near-contemporary description of the cult site of the god-name's continental form.[^3] The Norse literary witnesses are the Codex Regius, which carries Grímnismál, and the fourteenth-century codices of the Prose Edda. The Younger Futhark rendering ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ is a normalized reconstruction of how the name would have been carved; no Viking-Age inscription of the theonym is known.[^1]

Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Hall (D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Forseti.

meditation.body:
Forseti is the patron of the outcome the sagas almost never reach: the quarrel that ends. The heroic literature of the North is a literature of feud — insult answered by wound, wound by killing, killing by lawsuit, lawsuit by ambush — and into that world the Edda sets one shining hall where the arithmetic stops.[^1]

All who come with their cases go away reconciled: it is the only perfect record in the corpus, and it belongs to the son of the god whose own judgments could not stand. The tradition seems to know what it was asking. Reconciliation is not the absence of justice but its completion — the verdict both parties can live inside — and the god who delivers it is given nothing else: no weapon, no journey, no death, no prophecy. His silence is the teaching. In a mythology that counts its heroes by what they break, Forseti counts by what he puts to sleep.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 32; Grímnismál 15, trans. Faulkes (1987) and Larrington (2014).

poetic-edda.body:
The Poetic Edda's whole testimony to Forseti is one stanza, and it is the load-bearing one. Grímnismál 15, in Óðinn's tally of the dwellings of the gods, gives him the tenth: ‘Glitnir is the tenth; it is propped with gold and thatched with silver too, and there Forseti dwells most days and puts all suits to sleep.’[^1]

Every word earns its place. *Svæfir* — ‘puts to sleep’, lulls — is the verb of a nurse with a restless child, not of a judge with a gavel, and *sakir* covers the whole range of suits, charges, and quarrels the thing-assemblies knew. The stanza gives him no weapon, no journey, no adversary, and no other appearance anywhere in the poetic corpus: Völuspá does not name him among the gods of the last day, Lokasenna does not seat him at the feast, and no poem stages him in action.[^2] Snorri understood the stanza's authority: when Gylfaginning makes its one-sentence portrait of the god, it closes by quoting these very lines as proof — ‘as it is said here’.[^3]

sources.citation: Grímnismál 15 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Forseti.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 32, trans. Faulkes (1987).

prose-edda.body:
The Prose Edda is Forseti's great and nearly only witness, and it builds his hall twice. In Gylfaginning's survey of the heavenly places (ch. 17), Glitnir stands among the dwellings of the gods with walls, pillars, and posts of red gold and a roof of silver.[^1] In the catalogue of the Æsir (ch. 32), Snorri names the owner and states the office in one sentence: the son of [[baldr|Baldr]] and [[nanna|Nanna]], daughter of Nep, is called Forseti; he owns that hall in heaven which is called Glitnir; and all who come to him with lawsuits go away reconciled — ‘that is the best court of judgment among gods and men, as it is said here’ — and the Grímnismál stanza follows as the proof-text.[^2]

The placement is the commentary. Forseti enters the catalogue immediately after the sons of Baldr's generation — and the reader who remembers ch. 22 carries the contrast: of Baldr himself, Snorri said that none of his judgments can stand; of Baldr's son, that no judgment of his is ever refused. Elsewhere the Prose Edda keeps him in its systematic apparatus alone — the þulur count him in the roll of the Æsir — and Skáldskaparmál preserves no kenning-list for him: a god of one perfect record, filed with bureaucratic fidelity.[^3]

Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 32, trans. Faulkes (1987).

runic-evidence.body:
The runic corpus contains no invocation of the god Forseti. No runestone asks his favour, no amulet bears his name, and the name does not circulate in the Viking-Age anthroponymy the way the elements of [[thor|Þórr]]'s or [[freyr|Freyr]]'s names do — unsurprising for a theonym that is a law-title rather than a name-compound.[^1]

What the runic tradition offers is the orthographic frame. In the Younger Futhark — the sixteen-rune row of the Viking Age — the name would have been carved **ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ** (f-u-r-s-i-t-i): the ᚢ rune writes the o, the ᛁ rune writes both e and i, and because the name is a weak masculine ending in -i it takes no final nominative ᛦ. The rendering is a normalized reconstruction — no carving of the theonym survives — and the manuscript spelling of the Eddas remains the primary witness.[^2] The onomastic ground evidence belongs to the place-name record instead: Forsetlund, ‘Forseti's grove’, in Vestfold, is the cult-geographical trace the stones do not supply.[^3]

Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957), on the Younger Futhark.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Hall (D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Forseti.

sagas.body:
Forseti has no saga — but his name has a continental history older than the sagas. Around 796, Alcuin's Life of Willibrord records how the missionary was driven ashore on a Frisian island ‘called Fosetesland after the god Fosite, whom those peoples worship’ — Heligoland, the holy land. The island kept a sacred spring whose water might be drawn only in silence, and cattle that might not be touched; Willibrord baptized three men in the spring and slaughtered the herd for food, and when the islanders saw no judgment fall from heaven they brought the company before King Radbod, who cast lots daily for three days. The lot never fell on Willibrord; one of his companions was chosen and died for the sacrilege.[^1]

Later Frisian tradition kept the shape of a divine lawgiver. The late medieval legend of the law-speakers tells how the Frisians, wanting law, were set adrift in a boat, and how a thirteenth man appeared among the twelve, steered them to land, threw a golden axe ashore — where it struck, a spring burst forth — and taught them the law. Jacob Grimm could not keep the tale away from Fosite; modern scholarship generally reads the thirteenth as Christ.[^2] In the Norse book-world, meanwhile, the god stays inside the Eddic corpus: no saga of Icelanders summons him, and his living afterlife is the title — *forseti*, the presiding judge of the law-term, and in the end the president of a republic.[^3]

sources.citation: Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi 10, ed. Levison, MGH SRM 7 (1920).
Grimm, Jacob, Teutonic Mythology, trans. Stallybrass (George Bell, 1882–88), on Fosite and the law-speaker legend.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. forseti.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Forseti** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius (Grímnismál) and the codices of the Prose Edda, recording material centuries older.[^1] The manuscript form is itself plain ASCII: Old Norse writes no diacritic in this name, and the restoration changes nothing but the capital. In the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved **ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ** (f-u-r-s-i-t-i): the runic row underspecifies what the manuscripts fix, with ᚢ writing the o, ᛁ writing both e and i, and no final ᛦ, because the weak masculine ends in -i rather than the nominative -r.[^2]

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is a transparent compound: *for* ‘before’ + *seti* ‘sitter’ (cf. *sitja*, ‘to sit’), a weak masculine in -i with genitive *Forseta*.
- Old Norse orthography requires no accent: all three vowels are short, and short vowels carry no mark.
- The Frisian form *Fosite* (Alcuin, c. 796) is not derivable from the Old Norse compound — the crux of the borrowing question the handbooks keep open.[^3]
- The Unicode restoration Forseti is therefore identical to the ASCII form — a Tier 2 name by the mechanical rule, whose dignity comes from the office it names, not from rescued diacritics.

PuniCodex holds no domain for this name: the plain-ASCII **forseti.com** is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release.
